title: Designing From Production Experience

sections.title: Objectives That Count the Customer’s Attempt
A Durable Checkout Across Several Services
When Does a Provider Slot Become Free?
A Deadline Shared Across the Checkout
Release Gates for a New Region
Rehearsing the Failure, Not Just the Restart

html:
During Baodium’s European launch review, an engineer pointed to the two regions on the architecture diagram and asked a question that changed the meeting.

“If Europe’s write path fails at 14:05, can North America accept the next payment at 14:06?”

Both regions had application services and PostgreSQL databases. Asynchronous replication copied changes between them, and each region could reach the payment provider. The diagram looked like a system that could continue operating after a regional failure. Nobody could yet say whether North America would know about a payment that Europe had authorized just before losing connectivity.

Suppose the provider accepted an authorization at 14:04:59. Payment Service committed its result in Europe, but the corresponding database record had not reached North America when the region failed. If the customer retried through North America, what would stop another authorization? An account record on the surviving replica might show the earlier checkout as pending or might contain no checkout record at all.

The question drew on several decisions from earlier chapters. Chapter 3 established durable operation identities and reconciliation for uncertain payments. Chapter 7 examined replication and the transfer of write authority. Chapter 9 gave shared dependencies admission budgets, and Chapter 10 required evidence before a deployment could advance. The European launch needed those decisions to agree with one another under a regional failure.

This final chapter follows the design review from its first diagram to the revised architecture, the capacity calculations, and the failure rehearsals. We will also return to the five questions introduced at the beginning of the book and use them to review a system we have not encountered before.

The First Two-Region Proposal

The initial proposal placed customer-facing applications and a database in each region. Requests could enter through a nearby gateway, and both payment integrations were configured to call the same provider. The engineers expected the surviving region to take over if the other became unavailable.

There were two gaps. First, the diagram did not assign authority for a customer’s order state. If both regions could accept writes after losing contact with each other, they could create incompatible histories for the same account. Second, a region could acknowledge an operation before its record appeared in the other database. A surviving replica would then be missing information needed to recover an external payment effect.

Adding another database replica would not answer either question. The team had to define what it promised customers, where authoritative records were created, and what the application would do when that authority was unavailable. Only then could the engineers decide how much failover was possible.

What the European Checkout Promised

For the first European release, Baodium deployed regional application services, Catalog read infrastructure, customer-state storage, event consumers, and payment integration. Static assets and eligible cacheable responses could be delivered through nearby content infrastructure. The product deliberately kept recommendations, generated explanations, notifications, and analytics outside the synchronous checkout path.

An account had one designated write-owning region. Visiting another region did not silently change that ownership. This reduced the number of cross-region write cases the launch had to support, although it meant some customers could experience additional network latency when traveling.

The product owner also defined the meaning of a confirmed purchase. Order Service could report confirmed only after it had recorded the accepted order, a valid inventory allocation, and the payment authorization result. Capture took place later under the fulfillment policy. A confirmed order therefore did not imply that payment capture had finished.

A purchase could also be definitively rejected or remain durably pending. A pending response meant the application had committed an operation record, assigned a recovery path, and provided a status reference. Its next step might be provider reconciliation, fraud review, or completion of an inventory allocation.

The last row described a failure of the intended recovery contract. A customer could lose the HTTP response even when the server had committed a result, but the next authenticated status request should retrieve the original operation. Repeating a checkout submission with the same idempotency identity must continue that operation under its original parameters, rather than create another authorization.

Objectives That Count the Customer’s Attempt

The engineers carried forward the measurement boundaries from Chapter 8. Gateway response time began when the regional gateway accepted an eligible request and ended when the gateway completed or terminated the response. Browser reports provided separate evidence about what the customer saw.

The launch plan used four objectives.

  1. At least 99 percent of eligible checkout requests receive a confirmation, definite rejection, or durable pending response within three seconds.

  2. At least 95 percent of eligible checkout requests reach a final business outcome within three seconds. Pending responses are measured separately.

  3. At least 99.9 percent of distinct accepted checkout operations have a retrievable status within thirty seconds of acceptance.

  4. Payment operations pending longer than fifteen minutes enter recovery escalation. Elapsed time cannot turn an unknown authorization into a definite decline.

The first two denominators contain eligible gateway requests, including timeouts, failed responses, and disconnects. The third contains distinct accepted operations so repeated status requests and resubmissions cannot inflate its population. An accepted operation whose status cannot be retrieved counts against that objective even when the gateway responds quickly to other requests.

The product team added another guardrail. During a campaign, capacity rejections could not exceed one percent of eligible checkout requests in any ten-minute evaluation interval without triggering a product and capacity decision. A service can produce fast responses by rejecting most of its customers. Latency alone would not expose that failure.

A business rejection, such as a valid card decline, remained distinct from a capacity refusal. Both could be timely responses, while their effect on successful purchases was different. The launch dashboard reported confirmed, rejected, pending, and unavailable outcomes separately.

Tracing the Regional Request Path

With those commitments established, the team followed one purchase from the regional gateway to the systems that owned its business decisions. Figure Figure shows the revised regional serving layout.

The gateway authenticated the caller, retrieved the checkout operation identity, and routed the request to the account’s current write owner. Catalog reads could use regional replicas under the freshness rules from Chapter 7. Inventory Service owned reservations and allocation, and Payment Service owned provider authorization intents and their reconciliation.

The services did not all have the same failure response.

The distinction changed the code path. Checkout did not call Recommendation Service, even with a short timeout, because an optional call would spend part of the three-second allowance before its fallback ran. Recommendation generation and shopping-assistant tools also had separate admission allocations so a surge in optional work could not consume the workers or database connections required for orders.

A dependency labeled optional still needed an explicit outcome. Omitting recommendations was acceptable on a product page. Omitting an inventory allocation while reporting a confirmed purchase was not.

A Durable Checkout Across Several Services

The order workflow needed a durable starting point before any call capable of creating a financial or inventory effect. Order Service committed a record identifying the checkout intent, authenticated customer, accepted cart and price snapshot, and its initial state. Confirmation came later.

On the successful path, fraud evaluation assessed those accepted inputs. Inventory Service reserved stock using a stable reservation identity. Payment Service then recorded an authorization intent before dispatching to the provider. After authorization, the workflow completed inventory allocation and committed the confirmed order with its outbox event. The notification and analytics consumers proceeded independently under the delivery rules from Chapter 12.

No database connection was kept occupied while the application waited for the payment provider. This preserved the resource boundary established in Chapters 1 and 3 and allowed the payment attempt to continue through its own durable state.

A checkout could be interrupted after any of those steps. Recovery did not begin from the first step blindly. It read the recorded state and attempted the next permitted transition under the original operation identities.

One case mattered during the regional discussion. Suppose the provider accepted payment while the inventory reservation expired. The workflow could not confirm the order merely because an earlier reservation had succeeded. It had to retrieve current reservation state and either complete a valid allocation or create a compensating payment operation. An uncaptured authorization might be voided when the provider supported that action. A captured payment could require a refund. Each compensation had a separate identity and its own recoverable state.

The same rules applied after a region failed. A replacement region could continue the workflow only if it could recover the original records and establish the authority to execute the next step. An older replica that lacked those records could not safely start a fresh authorization.

Estimating Regional Database Capacity

Once the request path was defined, the team calculated capacity by resource and by deployment scope. Catalog provided a useful first example because the North American workload already had production measurements.

The expected European rate was 1,440 Catalog database reads per second. The corresponding North American requests occupied a connection for an average of 12 milliseconds. From Chapter 2, mean occupancy is arrival rate multiplied by occupancy duration:

1,440×0.012=17.28connections.1{,}440 \times 0.012 = 17.28 \quad\text{connections}.1,440×0.012=17.28connections.

That was a baseline estimate rather than evidence from European customers. The engineers also tested a scenario with 25 percent more reads and an 18-millisecond mean occupancy:

1,440×1.25×0.018=32.4connections.1{,}440 \times 1.25 \times 0.018 = 32.4 \quad\text{connections}.1,440×1.25×0.018=32.4connections.

The 18-millisecond duration was an explicit stress assumption. At a planning target of 70 percent utilization, the corresponding regional pool requirement was

⌈32.40.70⌉=47connections.\left\lceil\frac{32.4}{0.70}\right\rceil=47 \quad\text{connections}.⌈0.7032.4​⌉=47connections.

Why, then, did the proposed configuration contain eighty connections?

Catalog would run four instances, each with a local pool of twenty. Forty-seven was a regional estimate based on average occupancy, while eighty was the sum of four independently enforced process limits. A free connection on one instance could not immediately serve a request waiting in another instance’s pool. The extra configured capacity also provided room for uneven routing and the loss of one instance.

With one instance unavailable, three pools could offer at most sixty connections. The team tested that configuration at the expected European request mix, including acquisition latency and individual pool saturation. It also checked that database server capacity covered all configured pools across services, maintenance clients, and overlapping instances during deployments. A limit of eighty on the Catalog side was safe only if the database could support the resulting possible sessions.

Every capacity estimate recorded its input rate, measured or assumed duration, resource boundary, observation interval, and instance count. That prevented a regional average from being used later as though it proved that each local pool had spare capacity.

Payment-Provider Capacity and Recovery

Payment introduced a harder limit because Baodium did not control the provider’s execution capacity. The provider allocated 220 concurrent calls to the European payment workload, including calls initiated from North America during a failover. Authorizations, captures, refunds, voids, and status requests all consumed that shared allocation.

The payment team set a lower operating ceiling of 200 to leave margin below the external limit. It then allocated the 200 among work classes before calculating how many new authorizations it could admit.

Calculating Authorization Demand

The planned rate was 480 initial authorization attempts per second. For a stress test, the team assumed 25 percent more initial attempts during a campaign and another 15 percent from uncontrolled retries. At an assumed mean provider duration of 200 milliseconds, that produced

480×1.25×1.15×0.200=138concurrent authorization calls.480 \times 1.25 \times 1.15 \times 0.200 = 138 \quad\text{concurrent authorization calls}.480×1.25×1.15×0.200=138concurrent authorization calls.

The scenario was deliberately harsher than the production retry policy. During the campaign, the 25 percent increase would produce 600 initial attempts per second. The enforced retry budget allowed at most 100 automatic authorization retries per minute across the fleet, or about 1.67 per second. Under the same 200-millisecond assumption, mean demand would instead be

(600+10060)×0.200≈120.3concurrent calls.\left(600+\frac{100}{60}\right)\times0.200 \approx120.3 \quad\text{concurrent calls}.(600+60100​)×0.200≈120.3concurrent calls.

Neither calculation included calls still executing remotely after a local timeout. Both also assumed the provider’s mean execution duration would remain near 200 milliseconds. Those assumptions needed independent measurement during the load and failure tests.

The team reserved provider capacity for completing and investigating existing business operations.

The normal admission threshold of 140 was close to the uncontrolled 138-call stress estimate. With the enforced retry budget, the estimate of 120.3 left about twenty calls of margin below that threshold under the assumed average duration. The hard authorization cap of 155 permitted a separately approved increase without borrowing the other work classes’ allocations.

Reserved capacity had to be useful in practice. Fifteen status calls would not be enough if unresolved operations accumulated faster than status queries could complete. The recovery test therefore measured uncertain-operation arrivals, lookup throughput, age of the oldest unresolved payment, and repeated status attempts. New authorization throughput could be reduced to protect those operations when necessary.

Enforcing a Fleet-Wide Limit

Four payment processes with local limits of fifty calls each would permit 200 calls in steady state. A fifth process during deployment would raise the permitted total to 250, above the provider’s allocation of 220. Adding more processes could not increase the provider’s contractual capacity, so local semaphores alone could not enforce that boundary.

Baodium routed provider traffic through an admission and egress service that enforced the operating ceiling and its class allocations across the fleet. Payment processes had no independent provider dispatch path. Local limits still protected their own workers and connection pools, while the shared control determined which remote attempts could begin.

The egress service recorded the operation, provider account, attempt identity, admission class, and dispatch state durably before sending a call. Its admission and dispatch authority needed to survive failover without producing two active senders for the same work. The recovery procedure fenced the previous dispatch owner and accounted for attempts that might still be running remotely.

An asynchronous copy of admission counters alone was insufficient. If a replacement lost recent reservations while the provider continued processing their calls, it could admit additional attempts beyond the agreed ceiling. The new dispatcher therefore refused new calls until it could reconstruct active and uncertain allocations or establish a safe conservative bound.

When Does a Provider Slot Become Free?

A local timeout ends the caller’s wait. It does not necessarily end the provider’s execution. Releasing a shared permit automatically in a finally block could allow a replacement call to begin while the previous one was still active at the provider.

The attempt record distinguished a confirmed completion from an uncertain remote outcome. Uncertain calls retained their accounting allocation until provider evidence established completion or the documented remote execution limit allowed the system to release it safely. An expiring application lease could not provide that evidence by itself.

This policy may reduce new authorization capacity during a provider outage. The recovery allocation helps investigate earlier attempts but cannot compensate for an absent provider contract. If the provider gives neither reliable status evidence nor a bounded execution period, Baodium cannot promise both immediate reuse of capacity and a strict upper limit on concurrent remote execution. That limitation belongs in the launch review, with a tested procedure for the affected operations.

Retries and New Submissions

At the baseline rate of 480 first attempts per second, an uncontrolled 30 percent retry rate would add 144 attempts per second against the same provider. The production retry budget prevented that amplification by allowing no more than 100 automatic authorization retries per minute across the allocation. One designated component owned those retries so a gateway, mesh, and provider client could not each repeat the same call.

A new attempt refused before dispatch could receive a retry-later response, provided the application had established that there was no unresolved earlier attempt for the same checkout. When an authorization outcome was uncertain, the customer saw the existing pending operation. The system never interpreted an admission refusal as permission to start another payment identity.

Decision review

Who enforces the provider allowance?

The provider permits 220 concurrent European payment calls. Four payment instances run normally, and a fifth may run during deployment. An engineer proposes allowing each process fifty concurrent calls.

Use fifty local permits, because four instances permit only 200 calls.

Reduce the local limit to forty-four so five instances permit 220.

Use local protection with a shared, fail-closed provider-admission boundary that also reserves capacity for recovery.

The first choice permits 250 calls when a fifth instance starts. The second protects the arithmetic under that particular instance count, but four instances can use only 176 calls, and any scaling change needs a new calculation. Neither choice accounts for calls that continue at the provider after a local timeout.

The third choice enforces the actual shared allocation. It adds an admission dependency, so its failure policy matters. If it is unavailable or its active-attempt records are uncertain, dispatch stops until the budget can be established safely. Protected reconciliation and capture capacity cannot be consumed by new authorizations.

A Deadline Shared Across the Checkout

The provider limit constrained concurrent work. The three-second customer objective constrained how long the synchronous path could take. The gateway assigned one request deadline, and each required service received the time left under that deadline. A downstream call did not receive a fresh three seconds simply because it began later.

The first timing allocation was as follows.

The allocations add to three seconds, but they are upper bounds rather than fixed durations. Before dispatching authorization, Payment Service reserved time for recording the result and responding. It gave the provider the smaller of the two-second cap and the time remaining after admission and connection acquisition. Queue waits consumed the same deadline.

If the workflow could not finish preparation before the deadline, it returned the appropriate refusal or durable pending response without starting authorization. If it had already dispatched authorization, the expiry of the HTTP deadline left the payment operation pending for reconciliation.

Circuit breakers helped refuse later calls once the provider’s failure pattern became evident, but the breaker did not replace admission. In the first moments of a slowdown, attempts might still occupy the entire allocation before enough calls finished for a breaker to open.

Assigning Regional Write Authority

The meeting returned to the engineer’s first question. The surviving region could accept a new European write only after the architecture established that it was the current owner and had sufficient state to process the operation safely.

Baodium assigned each account or ownership group to one region. Its ownership record contained the group, region, state, and increasing epoch. Routing services used that record to find the destination. The receiving service checked the active epoch before changing authoritative state. A cached route could become stale and cause a rejection, but it could not grant permission to write.

The authority decision needed a control service whose own state was protected against conflicting updates. A quorum-based system such as etcd could store ownership records across separate failure domains. The deployment needed enough independent voters to preserve a quorum under the failures it claimed to tolerate. Two mutually isolated application regions could not each be permitted to elect themselves the surviving writer.

Having a tiebreaker location could help maintain a quorum after one region failed, but quorum alone did not fence a database connection or payment call already dispatched by the old region. The data and egress paths also needed to reject work under an obsolete ownership epoch. When the owner could not establish current authority under the approved policy, new writes stopped rather than creating a competing history.

A Planned Ownership Transfer

For a planned transfer, the engineers used the same controlled handoff introduced for merchant shards in Chapter 7.

  1. Mark the ownership group as transferring and stop admitting new operations through its old owner.

  2. Allow or resolve active source transactions, then fence the old database write path so stale workers cannot resume.

  3. Fence provider dispatch for the old assignment, retaining durable records of calls already sent and still uncertain.

  4. Establish the source’s final replication position and verify that the destination has the required order, payment, idempotency, and outbox records.

  5. Install the new ownership epoch and activate destination writes only after the old authority has been revoked.

  6. Verify old-owner rejection and the destination’s ability to retrieve and recover existing operations.

The fences have different scopes. A database epoch can reject a stale transaction, while the payment provider generally has no knowledge of Baodium’s regional epochs. Provider dispatch therefore requires its own egress authority. Fencing a whole region to move one account group may also interrupt unrelated accounts, so the enforcement scope has to match the ownership record being transferred.

If a required fence could not be verified, the destination did not open writes. A shorter recovery-time target could not justify allowing two regions to accept independent financial effects for one operation.

Unplanned Failure and Missing Writes

An unplanned regional outage removes the opportunity to inspect the old primary and establish its final WAL position. The surviving asynchronous replica may lack an acknowledged checkout, its payment intent, or an outbox event. Promoting the replica does not reconstruct those missing records, and it does not establish which actions the payment provider completed while the connection was lost.

The initial launch policy therefore did not promise lossless failover of payment and order state from asynchronous replication. Affected new writes remained suspended until the destination had sufficient evidence of acknowledged operations or had reconciled the missing interval. The application could continue serving eligible static and read-only features within their documented freshness contracts.

Zero loss of acknowledged state after a full regional failure requires that the relevant evidence be committed durably in another independent failure domain before the application acknowledges it. That adds cross-region latency and changes write availability when regions cannot communicate. The team documented the recovery-point objective (RPO) and recovery-time objective (RTO) for each important data class rather than assuming one pair of numbers applied to everything.

Backups served a separate need. A mistaken deletion can replicate to the standby just as a legitimate update does. Restore rehearsals therefore included point-in-time recovery and the business operation records needed to investigate external effects after restoration.

Operation Identity Survives the Region

The provider idempotency key identified a business authorization, independent of the region and ownership epoch that dispatched it. Region and epoch were recorded as execution metadata. A capture, void, or refund was a different business operation with its own identity, while a retry of the same authorization reused the original one.

The provider contract still needed inspection. If European and North American dispatch used different merchant accounts, the same text key might be unique only within each account. Failover therefore used the provider account and idempotency scope required to retrieve the earlier result. An uncertain attempt could not be sent through a different provider account as though nothing had been dispatched.

The provider’s idempotency retention period was also a recovery limit. After expiry, resubmitting an old key might create a new financial operation. The correct response then depended on provider status evidence and the documented reconciliation procedure.

Recovering Asynchronous Work

The order confirmation and its outbox record committed together. Relays, event consumers, and notification senders then followed their own durable processing contracts from Chapter 12. During launch review, the team looked beyond broker consumer lag to the age of the oldest unpublished outbox record, unfinished task, and unresolved provider submission.

One rehearsal introduced 40,000 queued events while producers continued sending new work. The recovery objective was to remove that backlog in twenty minutes without exceeding consumer and downstream allocations. That required approximately

40,00020×60≈33.3\frac{40{,}000}{20\times60}\approx33.320×6040,000​≈33.3

additional completed events per second above the ongoing arrival rate. A test that stopped producers before measuring drain speed would miss that requirement. A test that watched only Kafka lag could also miss notification tasks accumulating after event consumption.

The replay plan depended on the consumer. An analytical projection could be rebuilt in an isolated destination and validated before changing read routing. Notification replay could not resend old confirmations indiscriminately. Duplicate events and malformed records needed tracked outcomes under each consumer’s business contract.

Release Gates for a New Region

Baodium was introducing a new region along with new configuration. The team did not assume that every difference from North America indicated a regression, since traffic composition and network paths differed. Pre-launch tests established the European baseline. Later canaries were compared with stable instances in Europe, while absolute customer and shared-dependency limits applied throughout.

The first stage exposed five percent of eligible traffic. Promotion required two nonoverlapping five-minute windows with at least 2,000 eligible canary requests each. The router and replica count were configured to keep the candidate’s per-instance load representative, as Chapter 10 explained.

Relative comparisons were insufficient when versions shared a database or payment provider. A canary that increased database contention could slow stable instances too. A small difference between the two groups would then coexist with a customer-facing regression. The release checks therefore included regional totals, refusals, and absolute resource limits, including recovery allocations.

Removing canary routing affected future requests. Existing database transactions, provider calls, emitted events, and accepted operations continued through their ordinary completion or reconciliation paths. The team tested the earlier application version against records the candidate might already have created, because routing rollback could not undo a payment or an incompatible schema change.

Rehearsing the Failure, Not Just the Restart

Two weeks before launch, the engineers scheduled for production duty performed the recovery procedures using the access they would actually have during an incident. This tested whether the runbooks could be executed and whether the architecture produced the expected evidence. An exercise performed by the original authors with elevated access would have missed problems the on-call team could face later.

The lost-response test stopped Payment Service after the provider accepted an authorization but before the result was recorded. Recovery had to retrieve the result using the original identity. The inventory test expired a reservation while authorization reconciliation was underway. The application could not confirm the order without valid allocation, and any required compensation remained visible until resolved.

The regional exercise delayed replication and made the former owner unreachable. Responders had to show the destination’s known operation history and verify the enforcement path that prevented the previous owner from resuming. If they could not establish that fence, the test was a failed failover exercise, even if the replacement application’s health checks passed.

The admission test was equally important. A replacement egress service could not start with empty counters while previously dispatched provider attempts were unresolved. The event test checked downstream tasks and customer outcomes, not just Kafka offsets. The rollback test confirmed that older code could read and recover records written by the candidate.

The team recorded every failed step, the missing evidence, and the person responsible for correcting the procedure before launch. A runbook was considered usable only after someone other than its author had executed it under the intended restrictions.

What European Traffic Changed

After launch, production measurements replaced several North American assumptions. Catalog demand reached 1,692 reads per second, about 17.5 percent above the planning rate of 1,440. Mean connection occupancy was 13 milliseconds, giving

1,692×0.013≈22.0assigned connections on average.1{,}692\times0.013\approx22.0 \quad\text{assigned connections on average}.1,692×0.013≈22.0assigned connections on average.

A separate short-window peak reached 54 assigned connections across four instances. The engineers did not compare that peak directly with the 22-connection average and declare unused capacity. They inspected local pool occupancy, acquisition waits, traffic distribution, and the three-instance failure test. Fifty-four assigned regional connections could still coincide with one exhausted local pool.

The second lesson came from a Recommendation Service configuration change. One request class began fetching candidates in a loop, increasing its database queries per lookup from 1.0 to 1.6. Individual queries were still fast, and mean connection occupancy barely changed. The queries-per-request release gate detected the increase in both five-minute windows. The controller removed candidate exposure, and the team corrected the configuration before the next rollout.

The first campaign exposed a different assumption. Provider authorization p95 reached 1,900 milliseconds, compared with the 200-millisecond mean duration used during capacity planning. A p95 cannot be substituted for a mean when estimating concurrency. The payment owner collected aligned arrival, admission, completion, and duration measurements, together with outstanding remote attempts and refusals. The review checked whether capacity rejections exceeded the product’s one-percent limit rather than accepting quick retry-later responses as evidence of successful checkout.

Four authorizations entered reconciliation after their responses were lost. The workers recovered provider results under the original identities and checked inventory and order state before completing the workflows. Notification delivery also developed a campaign backlog, but confirmed orders remained available through their status endpoint while senders caught up. The notification owner measured delay through provider acceptance, not merely Kafka consumer progress.

The team updated the planning record with European observations, repeated the reduced-instance database test, and reviewed provider admission and reconciliation capacity under the observed latency distribution. The original calculations remained in the design history as estimates, with their assumptions visible beside the measurements that replaced them.

Returning to the First Architecture

The initial diagram made two application regions look sufficient for checkout continuity. The review established why that conclusion was premature. Regional routing, durable payment identity, provider capacity, and transfer of write authority all had to agree on what could happen after an interrupted request.

Figure Figure shows the major boundaries added to the proposal. It omits many ordinary application components so the write and recovery responsibilities are easier to inspect.

Now we can answer the engineer’s opening question. If Europe failed at 14:05, North America could continue serving eligible read-only traffic. It could accept a new payment for an affected European account only after the ownership and recovery requirements had been satisfied. If the surviving copy lacked an acknowledged operation and the earlier payment could not yet be reconciled, the safe customer outcome was pending or temporarily unavailable. The architecture did not promise an automatic new authorization at 14:06.

That was a deliberate launch tradeoff. The team preferred a bounded period without new writes to the possibility of authorizing the same purchase twice. A future design could seek faster recovery by changing its replication acknowledgment, provider contract, or ownership model. Such a change would need new latency, failure, and capacity evidence.

The Five-Question Design Review

The European launch needed regional ownership control, a shared provider admission service, and complicated recovery testing. A smaller system may need none of those components. We can still use the same questions to construct an initial design and decide when a new component is justified.

  1. What has the application promised? Define the accepted operation, its response deadline, and the evidence required to report success, rejection, or pending work.

  2. Which work can one request create? Identify downstream calls, retries, fan-out, and deferred jobs. Estimate their demand against each resource’s tested allocation.

  3. What survives interruption? Identify the durable operation, its authoritative owner, and the state needed to recover effects that may already have happened.

  4. What happens when a limit is reached? Decide which requests can be refused, which work can be deferred, and which resources must be protected for completion and recovery.

  5. Which evidence changes the decision? Record the measurement, denominator, interval, and action, including what to do when required evidence is missing.

Consider a service that accepts a document, extracts its contents, and makes the result searchable. The first question establishes whether 202 Accepted promises durable processing or merely acknowledges receipt by a gateway. That answer determines when the system must write its job record and where it will store the uploaded bytes.

The second question reveals extraction workers, object storage, a search index, and notification tasks. Those access patterns suggest object storage for the file, a transactional database for job state, and an index that supports document retrieval. There is no reason to make the entire request wait for text extraction if the product permits a pending status. The third question establishes how a worker resumes after a crash without uploading or indexing the same result incorrectly. The fourth gives the queue a capacity and admission policy. The fifth connects customer-visible completion to the state of the object and index, rather than treating worker uptime as success.

A booking service produces a different architecture from the same questions. Its essential operation may be reserving one scarce seat without double allocation. That guarantee points toward an authoritative transaction or other serialized allocation mechanism before we choose a cache, event stream, or additional region. Notifications can follow asynchronously, but the availability decision cannot rely on a delayed projection. Failure of the payment response still requires durable operation identity and reconciliation.

These examples do not prescribe the same set of components. The questions identify the guarantees and the operations that the components must support. We can then choose the simplest arrangement that meets the requirements, measure its limits, and add another boundary when the existing one cannot meet the promise.

Summary

Baodium’s European launch review began with a question about a payment one minute after a regional failure. The first diagram could not answer it because it showed duplicated infrastructure without identifying who could write, what state survived, or which provider effects might already have occurred. The revised design defined those obligations before promising regional failover.

Capacity estimates also needed scope. A regional average could conceal one exhausted pool, a local semaphore could exceed a fleet-wide provider limit, and a timeout could leave remote work consuming capacity. The launch team tested the degraded configurations and protected the work needed to finish or reconcile accepted operations. Release gates then connected the resulting behavior to customer outcomes instead of relying on healthy instance counts.

The architecture will change again as Baodium grows. Product requirements, traffic, providers, and the people operating the service will change with it. What matters is that the team can explain why each component is there, which promise it supports, where that promise can fail, and what evidence would lead them to revise the design. That is the work of practical system design.

Hidden assumptions

Assumption and scope & European planning begins with North American observations. Catalog uses four pools of twenty connections. Payment has a 200-call operating ceiling that includes protected recovery capacity.
Condition that tests it & European demand exceeds forecasts, provider duration increases, or a regional failure requires transferring a checkout’s write authority.
Constraint or invariant & Order confirmation requires recorded payment authorization and valid inventory allocation. Only the current owner may write. The old data and provider-dispatch paths are fenced before ownership transfers.
Evidence and uncertainty & The stressed authorization estimate is 138 concurrent calls without the retry budget and about 120.3 under it, against normal admission at 140. Still unknown: how long uncertain provider attempts continue remotely and which acknowledged writes might be absent after regional failure.
Signal and evaluation window & Observe customer outcomes, request classes, local and fleet occupancy, provider refusals, and pending-operation age through canaries, campaign peaks, and reduced-region recovery tests.
Control and decision & Revise allocations from European measurements. Pause or abort exposure on missing or failing evidence. Refuse new writes when authority or remote-attempt accounting cannot be established safely.
Owner and review trigger & Payment owns provider reconciliation. Inventory owns allocation. Release Engineering controls exposure, and SRE coordinates recovery. Review before campaign expansion, changing provider allocations, or regional transfer.
